candidates.statement: In section [\[necessary\]](#necessary){reference-type="ref" reference="necessary"} we describe a set of constraints which must be satisfied by the dihedral angles of any (not necessarily Delaunay) triangulation.
It is clear that there are certain linear constraints which must be satisfied -- to wit, for every face $t=ABC$ of $T$, we must be able to find angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$, such that:
The feasible region (set of solutions) of $L$ must be non-empty in order for us to have any hope of having a singular Euclidean metric on $S$ with prescribed dihedral angles.
In order for the linear program $L$ to have any chance of having a solution, the dihedral angles $\Delta$ must satisfy some constraints.
::: condition []{#dihpos label="dihpos"} All of the dihedral angles must be positive. :::
Furthermore, the sum of all of the dihedral angles of all of the edges of $T$ must be equal to the sum of all of the angles of all of the faces of $T,$ or $F(T) \pi$.

On the other hand, it is almost equally obvious that if $t_1, \dots, t_n \in F(T)$ is is some proper subset of the faces of $T$, then the sum of the dihedral angles at the edges incident to one of the $t_i$ must be strictly greater than the $n \pi$.

Furthermore, if $u_i^{(1)} = 0$ for all $i$, then the objective is non-positive, and is equal to zero only if all of $v_j^{(1)}$ are equal to zero as well -- this is so, since all of the $v_j$ must be non-positive, and all of their coefficients are positive, by Observation [\[dihpos\]](#dihpos){reference-type="ref" reference="dihpos"}.

It should be noted that the difference between the two arguments is largely superficial, since the proof of Theorem [\[maindual\]](#maindual){reference-type="ref" reference="maindual"} can be seen to essentially prove the Max Flow-Min Cut theorem.

candidates.statement: It should be noted the Theorem [\[infmain\]](#infmain){reference-type="ref" reference="infmain"} says nothing about uniqueness, and the proof certainly does not show any form of uniqueness.
Below, we show a negative result, which should be compared with the final example of [@rit]:

Combining this observation with Lemma [\[cona\]](#cona){reference-type="ref" reference="cona"}, we see that for any *Delaunay* triangulation combinatorially equivalent to $s(T)$, it must be true that $$\label{badineq} \sum_{v \in \{\mbox{old vertices of $s(T)$}\}} C(v) \geq \sum_{v \in \{\mbox{new vertices of $s(T)$}\}} C(v).$$ Combining Eq. [\[badineq\]](#badineq){reference-type="ref" reference="badineq"} with Eq. [\[gaussb\]](#gaussb){reference-type="ref" reference="gaussb"}, it follows that $$\label{badderineq} \sum_{v \in \{\mbox{old vertices of $s(T)$}\}} C(v) \geq \pi (|V(s(T)) - 2).$$ Note now that $|V(s(T))| = |V(T)| + |F(T)|$.

Now, if $T$ comes from a genuine hyperbolic structure, it must be true that the sum of the dihedral angles incident to the edges of $T$ must equal $2\pi$, and so for $T$ to correspond to such a structure, the following linear program must have a strictly positive solution:
::: theorem []{#hext label="hext"} In order for there to exist a weak linear hyperbolic structure for $(M^3, T)$, every normal surface with respect to $T$ must have non-negative Euler characteristic.
In order for there to exist a linear hyperbolic structure for $(M^3, T)$, every non-boundary-parallel normal surface with respect to $T$ must have strictly negative Euler characteristic. :::
In order for the primal program to have a non-empty feasible region, the objective of the dual must be non-positive.
In order for $(M^3, T)$ to be linearly hyperbolic, the objective must be strictly negative.
Hence, the new constraints simply says that in at least one of the old constraints the inequality must be *strict*.

Keeping in mind Remark [\[rmkkk\]](#rmkkk){reference-type="ref" reference="rmkkk"}, this implies that every non-boundary-parallel normal surface must have strictly negative Euler characteristic, thus proving the second part of Theorem [\[hext\]](#hext){reference-type="ref" reference="hext"} ◻ :::
